blocks.content: Picture a cruise ship crossing the ocean. Its hull isn't one giant hollow shell. It's divided into separate watertight compartments, sealed off from each other by heavy steel walls called bulkheads.
Hit an iceberg and tear open one compartment, and only that section floods. The bulkhead walls hold, water doesn't spread to the rest of the ship, and the vessel stays afloat and keeps sailing.
That's the entire idea behind the bulkhead pattern in software. Split your resources into isolated compartments so a failure or slowdown in one can't flood everything else.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396311132-418218516.png
blocks.alt: A ship hull divided into watertight compartments, with a flood confined to just one section

blocks.content: Bulkhead pattern: isolate resources per dependency or workload, so one overwhelmed piece can't sink the whole system.

blocks.title: Where the name comes from
blocks.content: Naval architects have built ships this way for over a century, specifically so a single hull breach doesn't sink the entire vessel. Software engineers borrowed the word directly because the failure mode it solves is identical.
1. Introduction

Most services talk to more than one downstream dependency. An API server might call a payments service, a recommendations service, a reporting database, and a third party shipping API, all from the same process.

If all of those calls share the same pool of threads or connections, a single slow dependency can quietly eat every thread in that pool. Once that happens, requests meant for completely healthy dependencies start timing out too, even though nothing is wrong with them.

The bulkhead pattern fixes this by giving each dependency, or each class of workload, its own dedicated slice of resources. A thread pool, a connection pool, or even a whole separate instance. If one slice gets overwhelmed, the walls around it hold, and everything else keeps running.
2. The core idea applied to software
blocks.text: 2. The core idea applied to software

blocks.content: At its core, bulkheading is just resource partitioning. Instead of one shared pool serving every caller, you carve out separate pools and assign each one to a specific dependency or workload.

The partition can happen at several levels. You can isolate thread pools inside a single process, isolate connection pools to a database or downstream service, or go all the way up to isolating entire service instances or infrastructure nodes.
2.1 Isolate resources per dependency

The most common form of bulkheading lives inside a single application. Instead of one shared thread pool handling calls to every downstream service, you give each downstream dependency its own pool, sized for how much concurrency that dependency actually needs.

["Thread pools a fixed number of threads reserved just for calls to one dependency.","Connection pools a fixed number of database or HTTP connections reserved per downstream target.","Semaphores a lightweight limit on concurrent calls, useful when you don't want a full dedicated thread pool."]
items: Thread pools a fixed number of threads reserved just for calls to one dependency.
Connection pools a fixed number of database or HTTP connections reserved per downstream target.
Semaphores a lightweight limit on concurrent calls, useful when you don't want a full dedicated thread pool.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396311133-709401815.png
blocks.alt: Two separate pools, one for a slow dependency and one for a healthy dependency, isolated from each other

blocks.content: 2.2 Isolate by workload or tenant

The other flavor of bulkheading isn't about which dependency you're calling, it's about who or what is generating the load. A reporting job, a batch export, and a live checkout flow are all different workload classes, even if they hit the same database.

At a bigger scale, you can isolate entire tenants from each other. Give each large customer, or each workload class, a separate service instance, a separate database, or a separate set of infrastructure nodes, so one noisy tenant can never starve out the rest.
3. The failure mode without bulkheads: resource starvation
blocks.text: 3. The failure mode without bulkheads: resource starvation

blocks.content: Here's the classic scenario. An API server has one shared thread pool of, say, 200 threads. It uses that same pool for every downstream call it makes, payments, recommendations, reporting, everything.

One day the reporting database gets slow. Maybe it's running a heavy query, maybe there's a lock contention issue. Requests to reporting start taking 30 seconds instead of 200 milliseconds. Each of those slow requests holds a thread the entire time it's waiting.

Traffic keeps arriving. More and more threads get tied up waiting on the slow reporting calls. Eventually every single thread in the pool is stuck waiting on reporting, and there are zero threads left to handle a checkout request, even though checkout's own dependency is perfectly healthy.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396311133-819109566.png
blocks.alt: A shared thread pool completely filled by requests to a slow dependency, leaving no threads for requests to a healthy dependency

blocks.content: This is usually called thread pool exhaustion or resource starvation. The dangerous part is that it turns one unrelated dependency's problem into a total outage. Nothing was wrong with checkout, but checkout goes down anyway.

blocks.title: This is how one bad dependency takes down everything
blocks.content: Without isolation, the blast radius of a single slow dependency is the entire process, because every request competes for the exact same limited pool of threads or connections.
4. Implementing bulkheads
Implementing a bulkhead means deciding where to draw the walls, then actually enforcing separate, bounded pools of resources on each side of them.
4.1 Separate thread or connection pools

Inside a single service, this usually means creating one thread pool, connection pool, or semaphore per downstream dependency, each sized based on how much concurrency that dependency can realistically handle and how critical it is.

Notice that reporting only gets 10 concurrent slots. If reporting slows down, at most 10 threads or calls ever get stuck waiting on it. The other 50 slots reserved for payments are untouched and keep serving normally.
4.2 Separate instances or nodes

At a coarser level, you can skip in-process pools entirely and isolate by deploying separate instances. A dedicated reporting service, a dedicated fleet of nodes per large tenant, or a dedicated database per workload class.

This costs more in infrastructure, but the isolation is stronger. A memory leak or a crash in one instance can't touch resources belonging to another instance at all, since they're not even sharing the same process or machine.
5. Bulkheads, circuit breakers, and timeouts
Bulkheads rarely show up alone. They're usually paired with a timeout and a circuit breaker, and each of the three solves a different part of the same problem.

["Timeout caps how long any single call is allowed to wait, so one request can't hang forever.","Circuit breaker notices a dependency is failing repeatedly and stops calling it for a while, so you don't keep sending doomed requests.","Bulkhead limits how many requests can be in flight to a dependency at once, so even while it's still being called, it can't consume unlimited resources."]
items: Timeout caps how long any single call is allowed to wait, so one request can't hang forever.
Circuit breaker notices a dependency is failing repeatedly and stops calling it for a while, so you don't keep sending doomed requests.
Bulkhead limits how many requests can be in flight to a dependency at once, so even while it's still being called, it can't consume unlimited resources.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396311134-190494815.png
blocks.alt: A request passing through a timeout, then a circuit breaker, then a bulkhead, before reaching a downstream dependency

blocks.content: Think of it this way: the circuit breaker decides whether to call a dependency at all. The bulkhead decides how much of your resources that dependency is allowed to occupy while it's still being called. You want both, because a breaker takes time to trip, and during that window the bulkhead is what keeps the damage contained.

blocks.title: They solve different failure windows
blocks.content: A circuit breaker protects you after a dependency has clearly failed enough times to trip. A bulkhead protects you the entire time before that, while calls are still slow but haven't failed outright yet.
6. Real world usage
Bulkheading shows up at every layer of a real system, from a single library call inside a process, all the way up to how you lay out infrastructure across an entire cluster.
6.1 resilience4j's bulkhead module

resilience4j, a popular Java resilience library, ships a dedicated bulkhead module with two flavors. A semaphore based bulkhead that just limits concurrent calls, and a thread pool based bulkhead that runs calls on a separate, bounded executor.

The annotation form is popular in Spring Boot services because it lets you attach a bulkhead to a single method with almost no boilerplate, while keeping every dependency's limits configured separately in one place.
6.2 Kubernetes as an infrastructure level bulkhead
blocks.text: 6.2 Kubernetes as an infrastructure level bulkhead

blocks.content: Resource requests and limits on a Kubernetes pod are a bulkhead at the infrastructure layer. Capping how much CPU and memory a pod can consume stops one noisy or leaking pod from starving every other pod scheduled on the same node.

resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "250m"
    memory: "256Mi"
  limits:
    cpu: "500m"
    memory: "512Mi"

blocks.content: Separate node pools push the same idea further. Instead of every workload sharing one pool of machines, you dedicate a node pool per tenant or per workload class, so a spike in one tenant's traffic can't take CPU or memory away from another tenant entirely.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396311134-66504408.png
blocks.alt: Two tenants each running on their own dedicated node pool, sharing only a common control plane

blocks.content: 6.3 Separate database connection pools per service
blocks.text: 6.3 Separate database connection pools per service

blocks.content: Connection pools to a database are a classic bulkhead target. If every service in your company shares one connection pool to a database, a slow query from one service can exhaust every available connection, locking out every other service.

Giving each service, or each workload inside a service, its own dedicated pool means a runaway query in one place can only ever exhaust that one pool's connections, never the whole database's capacity.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396311135-477766530.png
blocks.alt: Two services each holding their own dedicated connection pool into a shared database

blocks.content: 7. Worked example: reporting versus checkout

Say you run an e commerce API server. It exposes fast core endpoints like checkout and add to cart, and it also exposes a reporting endpoint that runs heavier aggregation queries for the seller dashboard.

Without bulkheading, both endpoints share the same thread pool. A seller opens the dashboard, triggers a handful of slow reporting queries, and now checkout requests are stuck waiting behind them for threads that never free up.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396311136-557935345.png
blocks.alt: A reporting traffic spike contained to its own pool, leaving the checkout pool unaffected

blocks.content: The fix is to give reporting its own dedicated, deliberately small thread pool, separate from the pool serving checkout and other core endpoints.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396311136-174342733.png
blocks.alt: An API server routing checkout traffic through a core thread pool and reporting traffic through a separate reporting thread pool

blocks.title: What this buys you
blocks.text: If reporting queries suddenly take 20 seconds each, at most 10 threads ever get tied up. Checkout keeps its full 150 threads and users checking out never notice the reporting spike happened at all.

blocks.content: 8. The interview angle
A very common system design interview question is some version of, how do you stop one slow dependency from taking down your entire service. Bulkheading is the direct answer.

The strongest version of that answer names the pattern, explains that it isolates resources per dependency or workload, and pairs it with timeouts and circuit breakers to cover the full picture, not just one of the three.

{"headers":["Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["Contains a slow or failing dependency's blast radius","More moving pieces to configure and monitor"],["Healthy dependencies keep working during a partial outage","Pool sizes need tuning, too small wastes capacity, too big defeats the isolation"],["Works at every layer, in process pools up to whole node pools","Adds a small amount of latency and complexity to every call path"]]}

blocks.title: Don't over isolate
blocks.content: Splitting every single dependency into its own tiny pool adds real operational overhead. Reserve dedicated bulkheads for dependencies that are actually risky, slow, flaky, or high volume, and let low risk calls share a pool.
9. Summary

A ship survives a hull breach because its compartments are sealed off from each other. A well built service survives a slow dependency for exactly the same reason, its resources are sealed off into separate pools.

["Bulkhead: isolate resources, thread pools, connection pools, or instances, per dependency or workload.","Without it, one slow dependency exhausts a shared pool and starves every other request, a failure called resource starvation or thread pool exhaustion.","Pairs naturally with timeouts and circuit breakers, each protecting a different part of the same call path.","Shows up everywhere, resilience4j's bulkhead module, Kubernetes resource limits and node pools, and dedicated database connection pools per service."]
items: Bulkhead: isolate resources, thread pools, connection pools, or instances, per dependency or workload.
Without it, one slow dependency exhausts a shared pool and starves every other request, a failure called resource starvation or thread pool exhaustion.
Pairs naturally with timeouts and circuit breakers, each protecting a different part of the same call path.
Shows up everywhere, resilience4j's bulkhead module, Kubernetes resource limits and node pools, and dedicated database connection pools per service.
